items.title: Pinned local-model digest mismatch on a fresh install: the installer flags a security event and continues
items.body:
A fresh consumer install pulls the local model and finds the content digest does not match what the release pinned:

```
expected: sha256:66c4f325bc71350f07fb2da4f92455553c7bbc8af5d7ee2095fbeac79b9e66c9
actual:   sha256:b9c79f8f56a90a86860d20d8025fde1ac0c03ef282b4f439b271abb7e8c72624
```

The installer's own wording:

> The upstream model was republished, or the download differs from what this release pinned. The model still works, but its behaviour is no longer the version this install was tested against. **Treat as a security event and re-run the tool evaluation before relying on it.**

`docker model ls` confirms the pulled model was created **9 days ago**, while the pin was captured 2026-08-16.

## Why this happens

This is the only tier pulled from HuggingFace (`hf.co/ggml-org/...`) rather than the curated `ai/` namespace. `local-model-policy.ts` documents the compromise:

> Pulled from HuggingFace, not the curated `ai/` namespace — `ai/qwen3.8` publishes only the 2.4T-A95B "Max" (1.31 TB). ggml-org is llama.cpp's own org, i.e. first-party to the runtime DMR embeds. Revisit if/when an `ai/qwen3.8:27b` tag lands.

A third-party namespace can republish a tag under the operator's feet, and it did. The detection works exactly as designed; the exposure is real.

## The gap

The installer **warns and continues**. A non-technical operator on the GA path sees a wall of `[!]` lines and a successful finish, and has no way to judge "treat as a security event". Nothing blocks, and nothing records the mismatch for later audit.

Options worth weighing:

1. **Refresh the pin** if the republished digest is trusted, and add a check that alerts when upstream moves — the pin is currently a snapshot that silently rots.
2. **Fail closed on `-Headless`**, where no human is present to read the warning, while allowing an interactive operator to accept.
3. **Record the mismatch as a governed finding** so it survives the install log and appears in the trust/evidence surface, rather than scrolling past.

Related: the same tier registers under a different runtime name than it is pulled by (`hf.co/...` pulled, `huggingface.co/...` registered), which the code comments predicted.

Provenance: from-scratch reset/dogfood cycle 4, image v2026.08.23-cycle4.1, local log IMP-098.

items.title: Six surface tools were added to the unconditional always-include set, putting a floor of 7 under the attached surface that the local gate does not honour
items.body:
## Observed

`selectCoworkerToolBudget` attaches anything in `alwaysIncludeNames` without consulting the cap:

```ts
if (always.has(entry.t.name)) { attached.push(entry); attachedCount++; }
else if (attachedCount < cap) { ... }
```

Both call sites pass `new Set([LOAD_TOOLS_TOOL_NAME, ...AUTHORIZED_SURFACE_TOOL_NAMES])`. `AUTHORIZED_SURFACE_TOOL_NAMES` holds six entries (`surface_list`, `surface_open`, `surface_snapshot`, `surface_query`, `surface_act`, `surface_close`). With `load_tools` prepended when anything defers, the attached surface therefore has a hard floor of **7**, whatever the cap says.

Modelled against the exact loop and ranking:

```
cap | attached | +load_tools | gate | verdict
4   | 6        | 7           | 4    | EXCEEDS gate
6   | 6        | 7           | 6    | EXCEEDS gate
7   | 6        | 7           | 7    | ok
15  | 14       | 15          | 15   | ok
48  | 47       | 48          | 48   | ok
```

Any cap below 7 produces a surface `callWithFallbackChain` refuses, which removes local from the fallback chain — the `BI-A8BFEFCE` failure, one layer further down.

## Reachability, stated honestly

This was **unreachable** until now: `MIN_COWORKER_ATTACHED_TOOLS` floored the cap at 12, comfortably above 7.

`BI-8634F0BE` (PR #4687, in the merge queue as of filing) corrects the floor so a measured tool-fidelity ceiling below 12 is honoured. That is the right fix for its own defect, and it makes caps of 4 or 6 possible for the first time — which makes this path reachable. Filed by the same session, against its own change, rather than left for someone to discover after the eval harness lands.

It still requires a local model measuring below 7, which is an extreme case. It is not urgent; it is a known hole that should not be left open.

## Cause: the comment records the intended design and the code drifted from it

The implementation comment states the contract:

> The always-include set (load_tools — the escape hatch that reaches every deferred tool) attaches unconditionally and counts toward the cap.

Singular, and for a specific reason: `load_tools` must survive any cap because it is the only route back to deferred tools. The six surface tools were added to the same set later, taking the cap exemption with them, and nothing flagged the divergence.

The same comment already names the correct mechanism for the surface tools two lines earlier:

> Tier-0 (page actions) keeps top PRIORITY within the cap rather than a free pass past it.

## Fix direction, not prescribed

Pass `AUTHORIZED_SURFACE_TOOL_NAMES` through `pageActionNames` rather than `alwaysIncludeNames` at both call sites (`agent-coworker.ts`, `autonomous-work-run.ts`). They keep tier-0 ranking priority — so on any ordinary cap they still attach first — but stop being exempt from the bound. `load_tools` remains the single unconditional entry, matching the documented contract.

Worth confirming while there: whether a coworker whose cap is genuinely below 7 should serve tool turns at all, or whether that measurement should instead exclude the model from tool-using work.

## Acceptance criteria

1. For every cap from 1 upward, `selectCoworkerToolBudget(...).attached.length` plus the prepended `load_tools` is less than or equal to the cap, except where the cap is below 1.
2. `load_tools` is attached whenever anything is deferred, at any cap.
3. On ordinary caps (12 and above) the attached set is unchanged — surface tools still rank first and still attach.
4. Both call sites are covered; the invariant is asserted on the ATTACHED SURFACE, not only on the derived cap, which is the level `BI-8634F0BE`'s matrix does not reach.
5. The implementation comment and the code agree about which names are unconditional.

Provenance: found by auditing whether `BI-8634F0BE` fully closed the invariant it was fixing, 2026-08-26. First modelling attempt inverted the tier sort and reported breaches at every cap; corrected before filing, and the real boundary is cap below 7.

items.title: Teardown safety stance says "no uncaptured work" while 75 of 98 open items exist in no bundle: the capture check compares COUNTS, not identity, so closing old work makes new uncaptured work invisible
items.body:
## Severity

This is the guard that stands between a reset cycle and permanent loss of the backlog. It is
currently telling the operator it is safe to tear down an installation holding **75 uncaptured
items**.

## What the operator sees

The workspace identity panel on this install right now:

> **Teardown — ALLOWED**
> "This is a development installation with **no uncaptured work**, so teardown and rebuild are
> routine."

## What is actually true

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Capture receipt `unfinishedItemCount` | **111** (captured 2026-08-24T06:13:10Z) |
| Current unfinished (`triaging`, `open`, `in-progress`) | **98** |
| Of those, created **after** the receipt was written | **75** |

**Seventy-five of the ninety-eight open items — 77% of the live backlog — are in no bundle**,
and the platform reports "no uncaptured work".

The bundle itself is real and was written correctly
(`/backups/backlog-captures/2026-08-24-pre-reinstall-final/`, 8 epic files). The capture is not
the defect. The **freshness check** is.

## Root cause

`apps/web/lib/install/instance-stance.ts`:

```ts
export function holdsIrreplaceableWork(input: {
  unfinishedItemCount: number;
  receipt: BacklogCaptureReceiptV1 | null;
}): boolean {
  if (input.unfinishedItemCount === 0) return false;
  if (!input.receipt) return true;
  return input.receipt.unfinishedItemCount < input.unfinishedItemCount;
}
```

The last line compares **counts**. It assumes the backlog only grows, so a count no higher than
the receipt's means everything is covered.

Backlogs do not only grow. Between the capture and now, items were closed, retired and deferred
while new ones were filed. The count fell 111 -> 98, and a **falling count reads as "more
captured than we have"** — the safest possible answer — at the exact moment the *composition*
changed completely.

The failure is silent, and it gets **more** likely the more triage hygiene an install does.
Closing old work actively hides new uncaptured work.

### The degenerate case

Close one item, file one item: count unchanged, receipt still "covers" it, and the new item is
in no bundle. Repeat indefinitely. The stance never notices.

## Why this bit here specifically

This install is a dogfood reset instance whose entire purpose is repeated teardown and
reinstall. The stance is the thing the operator is told to trust before the destructive step,
and it is also read by AI coworkers — it appears verbatim in the MCP server handshake as
`Teardown — permitted: ... teardown and rebuild are routine.` So an agent asked to tear down
would find no brake either.

Compounding it: declaring the installation identity re-evaluates the stance. Before declaration
the card read **CAPTURE WORK FIRST**; after declaring `evolve-dpf`/`development` it flipped to
**ALLOWED**. The operator experiences a normal configuration step turning a red light green,
with no indication that the underlying evidence never changed.

## Suggested fix

Compare **identity or recency**, never counts.

The receipt already carries `capturedAt`. The minimal correct check is:

```ts
if (input.unfinishedItemCount === 0) return false;
if (!input.receipt) return true;
// any unfinished item created or updated after the capture is uncaptured
return input.latestUnfinishedChangeAt > input.receipt.capturedAt;
```

Stronger, and worth the extra column: record the captured `itemId` set (or a hash of it) in the
receipt and return true when the current unfinished set is not a subset. That also catches an
item edited after capture, which a timestamp comparison on `createdAt` alone would miss.

Either way the invariant to state in a test is: **a backlog whose composition changed since the
last capture holds uncaptured work, regardless of whether it grew or shrank.**

## Regression test to add

Directly encodes the observed failure:

- receipt `unfinishedItemCount: 111`, `capturedAt: T`
- current unfinished `98`, of which `75` have `createdAt > T`
- `holdsIrreplaceableWork` must return **true**
- teardown stance must resolve to `capture-required`

## Related

- `BI-4884BE68` — teardown clears the model store each cycle
- The reset playbook already warns "this is a SNAPSHOT — re-run immediately before the
  destructive step". That advice exists because the product's own freshness signal cannot be
  trusted; fixing this removes the need for it.

Found during dogfood reset cycle 4 while testing the pet-rescue archetype workspace.

items.title: Local CI fences transient control-plane probe misses as sustained starvation
items.body:
Observed defect

The governed exact-tree local CI gate classified three runs of the identical candidate 286b14ef3e70bb55a11f7cbd3b9155cc0949d491 / tree 5710383fc383b621b68eeedd5da31c60bbdefb8e as blocked_control_plane_starvation even though the canonical portal remained healthy with restartCount=0, database/event-loop health was normal, Docker and PostgreSQL probes stayed healthy, and portal/MCP requests recovered immediately after each fence. One run passed all source checks, exhaustive tests, production compile, and reached image tarball handoff before a single MCP request miss fenced the build. The next two runs fenced after isolated short portal or MCP probe misses under dense lease renew / get_quiescence traffic.

Immutable evidence
- cmt7oe37a0awj01mgs5gb7j77 / NPEL-9DEB44EBC3
- cmt7on1ss0b1z01mgqignow0h / NPEL-CE0FF85D20
- cmt7otip20b4501mg6yzv4927 / NPEL-CA3B6E431A

Required outcome

Make the local-CI keeper/probe/fence contract distinguish a transient bounded request miss from sustained control-plane degradation, with explicit timeout ownership and deterministic consecutive-failure or time-window semantics. Preserve fail-closed fencing for sustained portal, MCP, Docker, or PostgreSQL failure. Preserve exact lease renewal/release and process cleanup; no orphan process and no product-gate weakening.

Acceptance
1. A deterministic test reproduces one 2.5-second portal or MCP probe miss followed by recovery and proves the build is not fenced.
2. Deterministic tests prove sustained or consecutive probe failures still terminate with blocked_control_plane_starvation.
3. Probe cadence, per-request timeout, grace/quorum window, and cleanup sequencing have one documented owner and do not amplify renew/get_quiescence load.
4. Existing source, exhaustive-test, production-build, Docker/PostgreSQL, and exact-tree gates remain unchanged.
5. After the repair is protected-merged, the frozen candidate 286b14ef3e70bb55a11f7cbd3b9155cc0949d491 is rerun exactly once under the repaired substrate.

Out of scope
- Editing the installed runtime
- Lowering or bypassing product gates
- Retrying the frozen candidate before the substrate repair
- Changing BI-86C5082D / WC-6A9A0D9D source content while this successor is active

items.title: A control-plane-starved local-CI run permanently wedges that branch and SHA from ever gating again
items.body:
## Problem

`projectLocalCiTerminalEvidence` (`apps/web/lib/gates/gate-run-identity.ts:117`) treats an evidence record as reusable only when `details.status` is `passed` or `failed`:

```ts
if (
  input.evidence.operationType !== "local_integration_ci"
  || details?.gateKey !== input.claimKey.slice("gate:".length)
  || (details.status !== "passed" && details.status !== "failed")
) {
  return { status: "blocked", reason: "mismatched-evidence" };
}
```

A run that ends in `blocked_control_plane_starvation` writes an evidence record with that status and **no `evidenceValidity.expiresAt`**. It matches on `operationType` and on `gateKey`, fails the status check, and returns `mismatched-evidence`.

The lease-claim path then treats that as a refusal to admit, rather than as "there is nothing reusable here, run the gate fresh". The record has no expiry, so it never ages out.

Net effect: **an infrastructure hiccup permanently bricks the change.** The gate can never run again for that gate key, and a runtime-code push requires a passing gate.

## The wedge survives commit rotation (correction, 2026-08-25)

This item originally implied that changing the commit escapes the wedge. **It does not.** Verified on this install:

- `git commit --amend` moved HEAD `02ef1084dbcc` → `26d51d8007ed` with a byte-identical tree (`66186cfbfcbc` both sides).
- The very next claim still presented `claimKey: "gate:7ab0ab8bbf9cfb53…"` — the same key — and was refused identically.
- `pregate:status` then reported `STALE` (record bound to the old SHA) while the claim path stayed blocked on the old gate key. The two surfaces disagree about what is wrong.

There are two distinct key spaces and they are easy to conflate:

| key | shape | derived from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lease claim key | `local-ci:${ownerSessionId}:${sha}` (`scripts/gate-worktree.mjs:813`) | session + SHA |
| gate evidence key | `gate:<64-hex>` (`lib/nonprod/local-integration.ts:114`) | **not** the commit SHA — stable across rotation |

So the escape hatch named in the original acceptance criteria ("no commit mutation") understates it: commit mutation is not an escape either. On the observed tree there was no governed escape at all.

## The existing rerun ladder does not cover this class

`scripts/gate-worktree.mjs:1384` already implements a retry escape:

```js
claimKey = `${baseClaimKey}:rerun-${terminalClaimAttemptSequence}`;
```

but it is guarded by `claimResponse?.error === "lease_terminal"` with reason in `released | cancelled | expired`. A `gate_evidence_blocked` refusal never reaches it. The ladder exists; it just does not extend to evidence-blocked admissions, which is likely the cheapest correct fix.

## Observed

2026-08-25 on `fix/deadline-tag-sub-day-precision`:

1. Run 1 ended `blocked_control_plane_starvation` at `local-ci-bounded-build` (`portal:request-failed`) while the host was loaded by an unrelated self-upgrade swap and multi-arch image pulls. The gate correctly classified this as *"infrastructure evidence, NOT a product build failure."* Everything before it passed: migrations, typecheck `classification=passed`, full vitest, `Compiled successfully in 115s`.
2. Evidence record `cmt9bs3s300ka01qvqgzelrga` (`ExternalEvidenceRecord`):

   | field | value |
   | --- | --- |
   | `operationType` | `local_integration_ci` |
   | `gateKey` | `7ab0ab8bbf9cfb53…` |
   | `status` | `blocked_control_plane_starvation` |
   | `evidenceValidity.expiresAt` | *(empty)* |

3. Run 2, control plane healthy (portal HTTP 200, all containers healthy, 23.8 GB free): refused with `gate_evidence_blocked` / `mismatched-evidence` before running anything.
4. `node scripts/local-ci-slot-cleanup.mjs --slot-key slot-0` reported `released slot-0 resources` and did not clear the evidence binding.
5. Run 3: refused identically.
6. Commit rotated to a new SHA with an identical tree. Run 4: refused identically, same `gate:7ab0ab8b…` key.

## Scope

A non-terminal evidence record means "nothing to reuse", not "never gate this again". The starvation classification is correct and worth keeping — it is what stops an infra blip being misread as a code failure. What is wrong is that it is durable, unexpiring, and treated as a refusal.

Options to weigh:
- Distinguish *no reusable evidence* (proceed to a fresh run) from *conflicting evidence* (refuse). Only the latter should block.
- Extend the existing `:rerun-N` ladder to cover `gate_evidence_blocked`, not only `lease_terminal`.
- Give non-terminal evidence an `expiresAt` so it cannot outlive the condition that produced it.
- Make `local-ci-slot-cleanup.mjs` clear or supersede non-terminal evidence for the slot, since operators are already pointed at it as the recovery lever.
- Reconcile `pregate:status` and the claim path so they do not report different causes for the same wedge.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run that ends `blocked_control_plane_starvation` can be re-run at the **same gate key** once the control plane is healthy, with no commit mutation, no tree change, and no force flag.
- A genuinely conflicting evidence record still refuses admission.
- The documented slot-cleanup lever restores the slot to a claimable state, or the docs name the lever that does.
- `pregate:status` and the claim path agree on the reason a gate cannot run.
- Regression coverage for the non-terminal-status path in `projectLocalCiTerminalEvidence`, which currently only pins `passed` / `failed` / missing / expired.

Found while gating a follow-up to BI-7CB2CCDE; that follow-up remains blocked by this defect. Related: BI-0F2A4137 (separate local-CI flake, same session).

items.title: A failed local-capacity probe silently disables the local inference fallback, turning a cloud rate-limit into an indefinite block
items.body:
## Observed

A workroom review thread reported: the certified reviewer was reached, its cloud provider was rate-limited, and "the local fallback cannot run its 48-tool configuration". No review tools executed, so the required independent approval could never be produced and the work blocked indefinitely.

Live evidence from `dpf-portal-1` (2026-08-25T23:56–23:57Z):

```
[autonomous-tool-budget] agent="AGT-WS-REVIEW" authorized=86 attached=48 deferred=39 cap=48
[callWithFallbackChain] Skipping local fallback (48 tools > 15 threshold for small local models)
[agentic-loop] routeAndCall threw: All endpoints failed for external-mcp. Attempts: [
  {"endpointId":"codex","error":"Codex CLI rate limited: ..."},
  {"endpointId":"codex","error":"codex-cli pool exhausted — resets in ~30s"},
  {"endpointId":"local","error":"skipped local fallback: 48 tools exceeds threshold for small local models"},
  {"endpointId":"codex","error":"codex-cli pool exhausted — resets in ~29s"}]
[turn] agent="AGT-WS-REVIEW" executedTools=0 toolSurface=48 estToolTokens=11600
       ctxPeakTokens=544 surfaceZone=overload toolAccuracy=na
```

The local model was capable of this turn by a wide margin: DMR serves `qwen3.8-27b` at a 262,144-token context window, the tool payload was ~11,600 tokens and the conversation was 544 tokens. It was refused on a count, not a capacity.

## Evidence-backed cause

Two collaborating policies disagree, and the disagreement removes the install's only fallback.

1. `deriveCoworkerToolCap(servedContextTokens, opts)` (`apps/web/lib/actions/coworker-tool-budget.ts`) returns the full `MAX_COWORKER_ATTACHED_TOOLS` (48) when `servedContextTokens` is null, documented as "no local model in the serving path (a pure cloud turn) → the full 48".

2. `callWithFallbackChain` (`apps/web/lib/routing/fallback.ts:273`) skips every local fallback entry when the attached surface exceeds `LOCAL_FALLBACK_MAX_TOOLS = LOCAL_TOOL_SELECTION_CLIFF` (15).

`resolveLocalServedContextTokens()` (`apps/web/lib/inference/local-model-context-reconcile.ts:278`) returns null for several distinct reasons — models endpoint not OK, fetch throw/2500 ms timeout, no generation model in the list, outer catch — of which only one means "there is no local model". The other cases mean "I could not read it right now". Both collapse to the same null, and the consumer resolves that ambiguity in the maximum-risk direction: 48, the one value guaranteed to make the routing layer refuse local.

So a transient read failure about local capacity silently deletes local from the fallback chain. Paired with a cloud rate-limit, the turn returns nothing at all.

The flip is observable on one install, same agent, minutes apart, with no configuration change between:

```
23:58:51 [autonomous-tool-budget] agent="AGT-WS-PORTFOLIO" authorized=189 attached=15  deferred=175 cap=15
00:02:59 [autonomous-tool-budget] agent="AGT-WS-PORTFOLIO" authorized=189 attached=48  deferred=142 cap=48
00:07:43 [autonomous-tool-budget] agent="AGT-WS-PORTFOLIO" authorized=189 attached=15  deferred=175 cap=15
```

With no measured fidelity on this install (`ModelProfile.customScores` holds no `toolFidelity` key for the active local profile) the cliff ceiling is 15, so `cap=48` can only arise from `servedContextTokens === null`. The probe is the only input that varies.

The failure is also invisible: `resolveLocalServedContextTokens` swallows every error and logs nothing, so the degrade leaves no trace at the point of decision.

## Second, latent instance of the same invariant break

`deriveCoworkerToolCap` honours `measuredToolFidelityCeiling` and will attach up to 48 tools for a local model with measured evidence, while `callWithFallbackChain` hardcodes the raw cliff (15) with no fidelity awareness. The moment the fidelity harness measures anything above 15, the budget will attach more than the routing gate will run. The comment at `fallback.ts:270` asserts the opposite — "the coworker-tool-budget caps its total attachment to the same constant, so a budgeted surface is never disqualified here" — and that invariant is currently false in both directions.

## Why this matters more than a degraded answer

For an independent-review gate, "no model answered" is not a slow answer. The gate reads required evidence fields; a turn that executes zero tools writes no evidence, so the review requirement stays unsatisfied and the work stops until a human intervenes. A transient 30-second provider rate-limit becomes an open-ended block.

## Acceptance criteria

1. "No local model present" and "local capacity could not be read" are distinguishable, and only genuine absence lifts the attachment cap to 48. An unreadable/unknown local posture degrades to the cliff-safe cap so local stays eligible as a fallback.
2. Local presence is determined from a signal that does not depend on a single best-effort network probe succeeding within 2500 ms.
3. The routing-layer local-fallback gate and the attachment budget derive their ceiling from one shared function, so an attached surface produced by the budget is never refused by the gate — including when a measured fidelity ceiling raises it.
4. A degraded/unknown local posture emits one diagnostic line at the point of decision, so the next occurrence is greppable.
5. Regression tests reproduce the reported shape: probe returns null while an active local generation profile exists → cap stays at the cliff → `callWithFallbackChain` does NOT skip local.
6. Genuine cloud-only installs (no active local generation profile) keep the full 48 attachment and are byte-identical to today.
7. No change to authority: deferred tools stay authorized and loadable via `load_tools`.

Provenance: reported by a workroom review thread; reproduced against the live install from portal logs and DMR state, 2026-08-26.

items.body: Observed twice while gating fix/local-model-ux at exact candidate SHA 270c5fe21023b17788502bf96de486446b4dab4d. items.title: Local inference drops Anthropic-style antml tool invocations as prose
items.body:
## Problem

The governed external reviewer route can select the active evaluated Qwen3.8 27B model and attach exactly the two required initiative-review tools, yet the model may emit an Anthropic-style `<antml:invoke>` block as assistant text. The inference adapter recognizes OpenAI-native tool calls plus `<tool_call>` variants but not `antml`, so the agentic loop records zero authoritative tools and terminates unverifiable even though the invocation names an attached tool.

## Immutable evidence

- `TR-MCP-Y210Nmg3bjg3MDBnYTAxbXhheDU2MXV2aQ-77B1C1EEF06B` at BI-9DC21917 design commit `4bfdf15434a0f38aa5c14d47d97123a40f83b6be`: local Qwen3.8 27B emitted `<antml:invoke name="read_source_at_version">...` as content; `executedToolCount=0`; no receipt/baseline.
- Dry proof `TR-MCP-Y210Nmg3bjg3MDBnYTAxbXhheDU2MXV2aQ-5CB0930C5194`: the same exact two-tool route returned “No provider-native tool mechanism is available in this environment,” again with zero tools.
- Earlier run `TR-MCP-Y210Nmg3bjg3MDBnYTAxbXhheDU2MXV2aQ-36CAFC14F74F` proves the same model and route can execute native structured calls, so model eligibility, tool grants, immutable binding, and source visibility are already established.

## Scope

In scope: deterministic normalization of a complete, well-formed Anthropic-style `antml:invoke` tool block into the existing internal tool-call shape, with focused adapter/parser and agentic-loop coverage. Authorization, grants, subject/org binding, sensitivity, writer authority, and argument-schema validation remain downstream and unchanged.

Out of scope: lowering the 70/70/70 reviewer floor, changing model scores or assignments, broad XML execution, interpreting malformed/partial invocations, changing reviewer policy, or auto-approving any writer.

## Acceptance

1. A focused red/green test reproduces the exact persisted `<antml:invoke>` form for `read_source_at_version` and proves one normalized tool call with the exact path/version arguments.
2. Multiple parameters, escaped text, boolean/number/null values, and deterministic call IDs are covered only to the extent the provider format actually emits them.
3. Unknown tools, malformed XML, duplicate parameters, truncated blocks, and content outside a complete invocation remain non-executable and fail closed.
4. Existing OpenAI-native, `<tool_call>`, and Gemma/Llama parsing regressions remain green.
5. A governed full-clone preview proves the exact BI-9DC21917 reviewer executes the immutable reader and writer through normal downstream authority; terminal prose alone is not acceptance.

Blocks: `BI-9DC21917` independent spec-approval/baseline recovery.

items.title: Local-only operation is blocked by paperwork: a zero-egress local runtime is denied code-gen for lacking DPA evidence
items.body:
A fully-local install cannot use its local model for code generation, and the reason is a missing trust attestation rather than any capability limit.

## Observed

```
[routing] no eligible endpoints task=code-gen sensitivity=development residency=any_enabled
  x cmt3gzbif09ow...: Provider 'local' is outside the request allowlist
```

The local connection:

```
providerId | status | evidenceStatus | executionChannel
local      | active | unreviewed     | local-runtime
```

## Root cause

`apps/web/lib/routing/provider-suitability/compile.ts` admits a provider to `allowedProviders` only when every connection's verdict is allowed, and a verdict requires `hasCurrentEvidence()`:

```ts
function hasCurrentEvidence(facts) {
  return facts.evidenceStatus === "operator-attested" || facts.evidenceStatus === "contract-uploaded";
}
```

A fresh connection defaults to `"unreviewed"`, so the local provider is denied.

## The inconsistency is in the same file

`compile.ts` already knows what "local" means and already exempts it from one rule:

```ts
function isLocal(facts) {
  return facts.externalEgress === "none" || facts.executionChannel === "local-runtime";
}

function regionEligible(facts, requiredRegions) {
  if (requiredRegions.length === 0 || isLocal(facts)) return true;   // <- local exempted
  ...
}
```

Data residency is correctly waived for a zero-egress runtime — nothing leaves the box, so there is no region to police. **The same reasoning is not applied to the evidence requirement.** A model running on the operator's own hardware is asked for DPA and processing-region evidence before it may generate code, when there is no counterparty to contract with.

## Why this undermines the sovereignty story

`local_only` is the strictest residency posture in the routing enum (`RESIDENCY_RANK.local_only = 2`). An operator who selects it gets **fewer** eligible providers than `any_enabled`, and if the only local provider is `unreviewed`, they get none. The strictest sovereignty setting is the one most likely to leave the platform with no working router.

Architecturally the path is otherwise complete: `ModelProvider.local` has `cliEngine = opencode`, and `opencode` is in `BUILD_ENGINE_IDS`. Local codegen is intended and wired. It is gated behind an attestation that does not apply.

## Proposed

`isLocal()` should satisfy the evidence requirement as it already satisfies the region one. If an explicit operator acknowledgement is still wanted, make it a one-click "this runs on my hardware" affirmation rather than a DPA-shaped form demanding a supplier contract id and processing region for a container on localhost.

Distinct from the first-boot enablement defect (the provider now ships `active`), and distinct from the model-selection question. Those are fixed or separate; this one is untouched.

Provenance: operator-identified during reset/dogfood cycle 3, confirmed unchanged on cycle 4 (image v2026.08.23-cycle4.1).

items.title: Registry acquisition strategy: let consumer installs upgrade from a published tag using the existing quiesce/rollback lifecycle
items.body:
The implementation item for the gap identified in `BI-DD7DC141`. Filed now, deliberately, because the design thread on `fix/consumer-agent-host` is correctly scoping itself to making self-upgrade *honest* (fail closed, report ineligible) and defers the actual mechanism to "a future artifact-upgrade BI". This is that item — an unfiled future BI is how a gap becomes invisible again.

## The insight

Self-upgrade conflates two separable things:

```
acquisition:  git fetch -> merge -> docker build a candidate
lifecycle:    quiesce -> recovery point -> swap -> health check -> auto-rollback
```

**The lifecycle half is install-mode agnostic and already good.** The operator panel advertises it — *"If an update fails, the platform restores the previous version on its own"* — and it already schedules against maintenance windows in the operating-hours timezone (*"next scheduled check: Aug 23, 2:00 AM CDT"*). None of that cares how the artifact arrived.

Only acquisition is source-specific. So this is a third acquisition strategy, not a rewrite.

## Scope

| Step | Source-backed | Consumer (this item) |
|---|---|---|
| Discover target | `git ls-remote` -> upstream SHA | registry: digest of the published tag |
| Obtain artifact | merge + `docker build` | `docker pull` |
| Deploy | quiesce -> swap -> health -> rollback | **identical, reused unchanged** |

The seam already exists: `apps/web/lib/queue/functions/self-upgrade.ts` branches on `if (config.sourceMode === "upstream")`, and `sourceMode` already carries several values. Add the strategy beside the existing ones.

Everything required is already present on a consumer install: it authenticates to ghcr (it pulls on every start), and it knows its own identity precisely — `v2026.08.22`, commit `a1184f557`, built 06:30Z. `Available: unknown` in the UI is one registry call away from being answerable.

## Pin to dated tags, not `:latest`

`v<YYYY.MM.DD>` is immutable and auditable. `:latest` moves underneath the install and makes *"what am I running, and what do I roll back to"* unanswerable — which the recovery-point machinery depends on. `daily-checkpoint-tag.yml` already cuts the dated tag and dispatches `publish-image.yml`, so the immutable identity exists; use it.

## Why not the alternatives

**Ship a git clone with consumer installs.** Turns every operator into a customizer — disk, git, and network they did not sign up for — reintroduces merge conflicts on an install nobody edits, and puts the memory-heavy candidate `docker build` on the operator's machine (it already needs a host-headroom guard on contributor installs).

**Leave consumer self-upgrade permanently disabled.** Honest, and it is the correct interim state, but it concedes that the GA install mode can never update itself. Given a fully automated daily publish already exists, that discards a working product story: *the platform updates itself overnight* currently benefits only contributors.

## Acceptance

- A consumer install resolves `Available` and `Target` from the registry rather than reporting `unknown`.
- An upgrade runs end-to-end through the existing quiescence, recovery-point, health-evidence and rollback path, with no new deploy machinery.
- Rollback restores a specific prior dated tag, not "whatever `:latest` was".
- The maintenance-window scheduling that already exists starts producing real runs on consumer installs.
- The manual `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d` currently required in the install directory becomes unnecessary.

Depends on `BI-DD7DC141` landing its fail-closed/honest-status change first, so the two do not fight over the same status surface.

Provenance: from-scratch reset/dogfood cycle 3; design reasoning recorded on BI-DD7DC141 with operator-facing evidence.

items.title: A docs-only PR boots a full portal: UX Route Sweep Runtime runs when the gate itself says it should skip
items.body:
A documentation-only PR (#4441 — one new architecture doc, one cross-reference paragraph, and the regenerated doc index) was blocked for ~30 minutes by `UX Route Sweep Runtime`, `UX Route Budget Sweep`, and `Merge Readiness`.

## The gate knows it should have skipped

From the failing job's own output:

```
::error::Exact-tree reuse expected UX runtime to be skipped
::error::Non-portal UX runtime concluded $RUNTIME_RESULT instead of skipped
::error::UX Route Sweep Runtime concluded failure
RUNTIME_RESULT: failure
```

The sweep gate correctly classified the change as **exact-tree reuse / non-portal** and expected the runtime to be skipped. The runtime ran anyway, booted a full portal, and failed — and the gate then failed *because* the thing it expected to skip did not skip.

So the skip decision and the job's actual trigger condition disagree. Every docs-only PR currently pays for a portal boot it was explicitly supposed to bypass.

## The runtime is also flaky when it does run

First attempt:

```
portal did not become ready within 120s
[runtime-capabilities] Startup reconciliation requires recovery:
  Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/dpf-state/runtime-transition.secret'
[embedding] Failed: fetch failed        (repeated, many)
```

A rerun of the same commit cleared all three failures with no code change, which is the definition of flake. Two separate defects therefore sit on top of each other:

1. **Mis-trigger** — a heavyweight runtime job runs for changes the gate has already classified as exempt.
2. **Flaky boot** — when it does run, the portal intermittently fails to become ready inside the 120s window, and the missing `/dpf-state/runtime-transition.secret` suggests state the CI environment does not provision.

Fixing (1) makes (2) far less costly, because docs and other non-portal changes stop depending on a portal boot at all.

## Why this matters beyond one PR

The required-check set for `main` is `DCO`, `Merge Readiness`, `UX Route Budget Sweep`. Because `UX Route Budget Sweep` fails whenever the runtime fails, **a flaky portal boot can block any PR**, including ones that touch no product code. Documentation, guard scripts, and CI config all inherit a runtime dependency they do not have.

The failure also presents badly: `Merge Readiness: FAILURE` is what an author sees first, which points at the merge gate rather than at a portal that would not start.

## Possibly related

The runtime log is full of `[embedding] Failed: fetch failed`, and PR #4440 (*"fix(embedding): a capacity deferral is not a model failure"*) is open against that same area. Worth checking whether the embedding failures are the cause of the slow boot or merely noise alongside it.

Provenance: observed on PR #4441 during reset/dogfood cycle 3; failure and clean rerun both on commit `92a4ffffd`.

items.title: deriveSkillCatalogCap reads the same ambiguous null and uncaps the skill catalog when the local window is merely unread
items.body:
## Context

Found while fixing `BI-A8BFEFCE`, and deliberately left out of that change to keep one concern per PR. The design doc records the boundary: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-26-local-fallback-eligibility-invariant-design.md`.

## Problem

`deriveSkillCatalogCap(servedContextTokens)` in `apps/web/lib/actions/coworker-tool-budget.ts` returns `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` — an uncapped skill catalog — whenever `servedContextTokens` is null or zero:

```ts
export function deriveSkillCatalogCap(servedContextTokens: number | null | undefined): number {
  if (!servedContextTokens || servedContextTokens <= 0) return Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
  ...
}
```

That is the same ambiguous null `BI-A8BFEFCE` fixed for the tool cap. When the local probe fails, the window reads as null, and the skill catalog goes uncapped on an install whose local model may well be small. The module's own header notes the skills catalog is the largest UNCAPPED non-tool block — a heavy coworker holds 36-38 skills at roughly 4k tokens.

`BI-A8BFEFCE` added `resolveLocalServingPosture`, which returns an honest `present | absent | unknown`, and `agent-coworker.ts` already has that presence in scope at the `deriveSkillCatalogCap` call site. The plumbing is done; only this consumer still reads the ambiguous value.

## Why it was separated

Different failure mode. The tool-cap defect made the routing layer refuse the local fallback outright, producing turns that executed nothing. This one risks context overflow, which has its own handling path (`describeContextCapacityFailure`, `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE`). Folding it in would have widened a targeted routing fix into prompt assembly.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `deriveSkillCatalogCap` distinguishes an absent local model from an unread one, using the same `LocalPresence` the tool cap consumes.
2. An unknown or present posture with an unreadable window applies the cliff-prone catalog cap rather than uncapping.
3. A genuinely cloud-only install (`absent`) keeps the uncapped catalog and is byte-identical to today.
4. An explicitly invoked skill is still pinned into the catalog regardless of the cap (`capSkillCatalog` behavior preserved).
5. Regression test covers null window with each of the three presence values.

Provenance: source inspection during `BI-A8BFEFCE`, 2026-08-26.

items.title: Local-CI queue loses dead-waiter reconciliation under load: a 10s MCP timeout on a call that normally takes 0.6s silently disables the only mechanism that reclaims a dead waiter's lease
items.body:
## Observed

Running `pnpm run pregate` on `fix/teardown-stance-capture-freshness` while another session held
the `local-integration-ci` lease:

```
gate-worktree: preflight sees 1 active local-integration-ci lease(s); claim will queue if busy.
local-CI admission queued at position 2; observing again in 9.2s...
gate-worktree: dead-waiter reconciliation unavailable
  (mcpCall: list_nonprod_environment_leases timed out after 10000ms); queue remains fail-closed
local-CI admission queued at position 1; observing again in 13.5s... (still; 8 polls)
```

## The endpoint is not slow

Measured against the same portal, same endpoint, same tool, no tier parameter — exactly the path
`scripts/gate-worktree.mjs` uses (`http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/mcp/v1`):

| Call | Time |
|---|---|
| `list_nonprod_environment_leases`, pregate's path | **0.62s** |
| same tool with `?tier=full` | 1.50s |

Both far inside the 10s default in `scripts/lib/mcp-client.mjs:75` (`timeoutMs = 10_000`).

So this is **not** steady-state slowness. The timeout fired under transient load — the portal was
simultaneously serving another session's local-CI run and browser traffic. Which is precisely the
condition under which the queue exists at all: reconciliation is needed most exactly when the box
is busy, and that is when the call is most likely to time out.

## Why it matters

The message is honest about the consequence — *"queue remains fail-closed"* — and fail-closed is
the right default. But it means the mechanism that reclaims a lease from a **dead** waiter is
silently unavailable. A waiter that died holding a slot is then never reconciled, and every
queued gate behind it waits indefinitely. Recovery becomes manual.

Every PR passes through this gate, so a stalled queue blocks all merges on the box, not one
branch.

## Suggested fix

1. **Raise or separate the timeout for reconciliation reads.** A read-only lease listing is
   idempotent and cheap; 10s is tight for a moment of contention. A distinct, longer budget for
   reconciliation (or a small bounded retry with backoff) costs nothing when the box is idle and
   is the difference between reconciling and not when it is busy.
2. **Retry before declaring it unavailable.** One timeout currently disables reconciliation for
   that poll with no second attempt.
3. **Escalate on repetition.** The line appears once and then the queue keeps polling with no
   further mention. If reconciliation has been unavailable for N consecutive polls while the
   queue has not advanced, say so loudly — that is the shape of a stall, and right now it is
   indistinguishable from a legitimately busy queue.

## Not a defect in the queue itself

Recorded explicitly so this is not over-read: the queue behaved correctly here. It queued,
reported position, polled with backoff, and stayed fail-closed when it could not verify. The
contention was genuine — another session legitimately held the lease. The only defect is that a
transient timeout removes a safety net without any path back.

Found during dogfood reset cycle 4, gating PR #4678.

items.title: Consumer installs have no upgrade path: self-upgrade builds from source, and there is no registry-based mechanism
items.body:
Every self-upgrade run on a consumer install skips. Verified on a fresh install:

```
latestRun: { runId: "SUR-16E9F749", status: "skipped", reason: "no-target" }
lineageSha: null,  pendingPrCount: null,  reason: "tally-uncomputable"
enabled: true, sourceMode: "upstream", routineUpgradeEligible: true
```

## Correction to the original framing of this item

This was first filed as *"target resolution requires a git source"*, implying the fix is to resolve the target from the registry instead. **That understates it.** Self-upgrade does not pull images at all — it **builds** them:

```
git fetch -> merge -> docker build a candidate locally -> swap
```

That is why the flow handles `merge-conflict` during prep, compares a `builtStamp` rather than a registry digest for its nothing-newer guard (`skipAttempt("up-to-date", ...builtStamp)`), and carries a host-memory-headroom guard because the candidate build is memory-heavy.

**The registry is not an input to self-upgrade.** So this is not a broken lookup to repoint; build-from-source and pull-a-published-digest share almost nothing, and a consumer install needs a *different mechanism*, not a patched one.

## Root cause — structural

`apps/web/lib/queue/functions/self-upgrade.ts`:

```js
if (config.sourceMode === "upstream") {
  await gitRun(buildFetchCommand({ hostSourcePath, remote, branch }).slice(1));
  const head = await gitRun(buildRemoteHeadCommand({ hostSourcePath, remote, branch }).slice(1));
  upstreamSha = head.code === 0 ? head.stdout.trim() : null;
  if (!upstreamSha) return await skipAttempt("no-target");
```

Confirmed on this install: `.install-mode` = `consumer`; no `DPF_HOST_SOURCE_PATH` in `.env`; `ls -d /host-source/.git` inside `dpf-portal-1` returns nothing.

Note the two distinct skip reasons — `no-target` (line 344, could not resolve what to upgrade **to**) versus `up-to-date` (lines 349 and 470, resolved a target and already have it). We hit `no-target`, so the run never reaches a comparison. This is a failure, not an idle no-op, and should not be read as "nothing to do".

## The consumer install has NO upgrade path at all

Not a broken one — an absent one:

- `dpf-start.ps1` contains no `pull`.
- `/d/DPF/scripts/` holds `bootstrap-organization-pki.ps1`, `capability-service-catalog.generated.json`, `installer`, `lib`, `pki`, `safety` — nothing that updates the install.
- The only way to move a consumer install forward is a manual `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`.

## The publish chain is separate, and it works

Worth separating so this item is not mistaken for the cause of a stale server. `publish-image.yml` triggers on `push: tags: ["v*"]` or `workflow_dispatch`, and runs daily by dispatch:

```
2026-08-21T07:26  workflow_dispatch  v2026.08.21  success
2026-08-20T07:25  workflow_dispatch  v2026.08.20  success
2026-08-19T07:22  workflow_dispatch  v2026.08.19  success
```

At time of writing the published `:latest` digest is byte-identical to the running image (`sha256:63eb23fd...`), so `docker compose pull` would be a no-op — while `main` sits **21 commits** ahead of `v2026.08.21`. Publishing is a daily batch, not continuous; that is a separate question from this item.

## What to decide

Consumer installs have an image tag, not a git lineage. They need a first-class **registry-based** upgrade: compare the running image digest against the published tag, pull, and swap under the same quiescence/recovery-point/evidence discipline the source path already has. That is a sibling mechanism to self-upgrade, not a branch inside it.

Minimum acceptable outcome if that is out of scope now: the status surface must stop reporting `enabled: true` and `routineUpgradeEligible: true` on an install where no upgrade can ever occur, and say plainly that self-upgrade requires a source-backed install.

## Related — one architectural question, not two bugs

The consumer-install agent-orientation item (`BI-11D611B3`) is the second surface where the GA/recommended install mode was not built for. Treat them together: the question is whether a sourceless consumer install is a first-class citizen — for upgrading itself and for hosting an external agent — and today two independent surfaces assume it is not.

Provenance: from-scratch reset/dogfood cycle 3, operator-reported; framing corrected after tracing the build path.

---

## Operator-facing evidence (2026-08-22, after a manual image upgrade)

The self-upgrade panel, on a consumer install now running `v2026.08.22`:

```
Self-Upgrade: Enabled (stable)              [ Upgrade now ]
Running:          a1184f557e35...
Available:        unknown
Platform version: v2026.08.22
Deployed:         a1184f557e358371a8ee9817ecece0a8eec26636 (commit)
Target:           unknown

Latest Run  SKIPPED  SUR-C0E89C42   Triggered by: manual
  No upgrade target — upgrade did not run.
  No target build could be resolved from the upstream source, so there was nothing to deploy.

What's in this update?
  Could not resolve the upstream target SHA.
  Confirm the host clone has a fresh fetch of the configured remote/branch.
```

Three problems visible in one screen:

1. **The button cannot work.** `Self-Upgrade: Enabled (stable)` sits beside an `Upgrade now` control that produces `SKIPPED / no-target` every time it is pressed. This run was operator-triggered, not scheduled — someone deliberately asked, and got a non-answer.

2. **The remediation text is impossible to follow.** *"Confirm the host clone has a fresh fetch of the configured remote/branch"* instructs a consumer operator to repair something that does not and should not exist on their install. There is no host clone. The advice is correct for the customizer path and actively misleading here.

3. **`Available: unknown` and `Target: unknown` are the actual gap.** The install knows precisely what it is running — `v2026.08.22`, commit `a1184f557`, built 06:30Z — and cannot discover what is available, because the only discovery path it has is git. The registry, which holds exactly that answer and which the install already authenticates against to pull, is never consulted.

The upgrade that produced this state was performed by hand (`docker compose pull && up -d`) after the daily `v2026.08.22` publish. The platform moved forward; its self-upgrade feature had no part in it.

## Trap for whoever implements this

`/workspace/.git` **does** exist inside `dpf-portal-1`, and it is not a source clone. It is the Build Studio sandbox: branch `my-changes`, **no remotes configured**, `git ls-remote origin` fails with *"'origin' does not appear to be a git repository"*.

Do not resolve the "no host clone" problem by pointing `hostSourcePath` at it. That would either fail differently or, worse, attempt to upgrade the platform from an agent's scratch branch. The absence of a fetchable upstream is real; a repo being present is not the same as a source of truth being present.

items.title: Install never provisions an MCP token, so an external agent has no way in — and the two scripts that would fix it are absent from the release bundle
items.body:
**Catch-22 on a consumer install: an external agent cannot obtain a token without a human using the portal UI, and the portal UI is precisely what an agent cannot use.**

## The installer intends to solve this and cannot

Verbatim from a real consumer install log:

```
[!] scripts\seed-worktree-mcp.ps1 not found; skipping MCP token seeding.
[!] scripts\dpf-bootstrap-agent-toolchain.ps1 not found; skipping agent toolchain convergence.
[!] Agent CLIs (Claude Code / Codex) will NOT be wired to this install's MCP endpoint.
[!] To connect one later: Admin > Platform Development > MCP, issue a token, then add the
    'dpf' server to your agent client's config using that token.
```

`install-dpf.ps1` calls both scripts. **Neither ships in the consumer release bundle.** `/d/DPF/scripts/` contains only `bootstrap-organization-pki.ps1`, `capability-service-catalog.generated.json`, `installer`, `lib`, `pki`, `safety`.

So the install degrades to a manual portal step. The README states that with Claude Code or Codex present the installer "wires them automatically — DPF skills, MCP tools, and kernel-tier memory all available on the first turn of every new contributor session." On a consumer install that is not what happens.

Note those two warnings only appear at all because of #4394 earlier in this cycle. Before that the skips were silent and this was invisible.

## The pattern to copy is in the same installer

```powershell
tsx scripts/issue-edge-bootstrap-token.ts --ttl-minutes 30 --auto-approve
```

The installer **already issues a short-lived, auto-approved bootstrap token** — for Edge Node enrollment. Exactly the shape required: time-boxed, scoped, no human in the loop, no long-lived secret written anywhere permanent.

`apps/web/lib/auth/mcp-host-writer.ts` already knows how to write agent host config, and the `.mcp.json` the portal produces is already correct — `Authorization: Bearer ${DPF_MCP_BEARER_TOKEN}`, secret referenced rather than embedded. Both halves exist; neither reaches a consumer install.

## Proposed

1. Ship `seed-worktree-mcp.*` and `dpf-bootstrap-agent-toolchain.*` in the release bundle. **Both halves are required** — the `cp` into `/dpf-release-assets/` AND the `COPY` into the init stage. A `cp` without the `COPY` fails the build; a `COPY` without the `cp` ships nothing. This is the same defect that left `uninstall-dpf.*` missing.
2. Issue a scoped, short-TTL MCP bootstrap token during install, write `.mcp.json`, and set `DPF_MCP_BEARER_TOKEN`. First agent turn then works; the operator rotates or revokes from Platform Development afterwards.
3. **Tier matters.** A bootstrap token should be `Observer` or `Development`, not `Admin`. An agent that can read the platform and propose work on first connect is useful; one that can administer it before any human has looked is not.

## Relationship to the agent-contract item

This is upstream of `BI-11D611B3`. That item asks *what an agent should be told* on a sourceless install, and leans toward serving the contract over MCP. **A contract delivered over MCP is unreachable without a token.** Whichever delivery mechanism that item picks, this one has to land first or the design does not close.

Provenance: from-scratch reset/dogfood cycle 3, operator-raised.

items.title: Onboarding never touches estate discovery, and a fresh install ships seeded estate data with zero connections
items.body:
Three from-scratch dogfood cycles drove install -> onboarding -> archetype configuration and **never touched estate discovery once**. Onboarding's eleven steps do not include it. That is not an oversight in the testing alone — the product surfaces it as a first-class capability and the guided setup omits it.

## What a fresh install actually presents

```
list_discovery_connections  ->  0 discovery connection(s)
summarize_estate_posture    ->  runKey DISC-1787515806258, status completed,
                                23 items, 32 relationships, 12 need review
                                issueGroups: taxonomy_attribution_low_confidence (3), ...
```

A **completed discovery run with 23 items and 32 relationships, and zero connections that could have discovered anything.** This is seeded demo data presented through the same surface real findings would use. An operator glancing at Estate would reasonably conclude discovery had run against their environment.

Ten tools back this area — `discovery_sweep`, `configure_gateway_scan`, `configure_and_test_discovery_connection`, `list_discovery_connections`, `summarize_estate_posture`, `list_patch_posture`, `review_estate_identity`, `update_lifecycle`. Lifecycle and patch posture are explicit, so end-of-life devices and pending upgrades are squarely in scope.

## The demonstration that makes this concrete

During cycle 3 the operator upgraded Docker Desktop by hand. The platform runs **on top of** Docker, claims patch posture and lifecycle as capabilities, and could not raise it — because nothing was connected for it to notice, and the estate surface was busy showing 23 seeded items instead.

If the platform cannot see the version of the runtime it is executing inside, that is the smallest possible test case and it currently fails.

## Two distinct defects

1. **Onboarding does not cover estate.** Eleven steps take an operator through business context, providers, branding, decision stance, hours, storefront, platform dev, build, COO and workspace — and never ask about the environment the platform is meant to manage. For an operator whose reason for adopting the platform is estate management, the guided setup never mentions it.

2. **Seeded estate data is indistinguishable from discovered estate data.** A completed run with 23 items and no connections should be labelled as sample data, or not present as a completed run at all. The risk is not cosmetic: an operator who believes discovery has run will not configure it, and will trust an empty picture.

## What good looks like

Onboarding should include an estate step that at minimum offers to configure a discovery connection, states plainly that none exists, and distinguishes seeded sample content from real findings. The connection step legitimately requires an operator credential (a network gateway key) — that is fine and mirrors the Build Studio OAuth boundary; it should be *asked for*, not silently skipped.

Worth deciding explicitly what happens to the 23 seeded items when a real sweep first runs: reconcile, duplicate, or sit alongside as permanent noise. Seeded data plus real discovery is where an estate either merges cleanly or quietly doubles.

Provenance: from-scratch reset/dogfood cycle 3, operator-raised. Now covered by playbook Phase 5.

items.title: Bound hung exhaustive Vitest stages in governed local CI
items.body: A governed local-CI run can hold the singleton lease indefinitely when Vitest leaves one live but idle worker after all test output. The stage receipt heartbeat stops, but local-ci-vitest-runner has no stale-heartbeat or wall-clock deadline; gate-worktree continues renewing the 2-minute lease forever because the child PID remains alive. Reproduced on frozen candidate 286b14ef3 under NPEL-79E8B0C233: exhaustive output stopped at 2026-08-25T01:16:40Z, stage heartbeat stopped at 01:20:48Z, while the exact worker and lease remained alive beyond one hour. Acceptance: use the existing observed-process/stage-receipt substrate to apply a bounded Vitest-stage deadline, terminate the child through the runner's own finalizer, persist an unambiguous runner-termination/retry receipt, release the lease, preserve one differentiated recovery attempt, and never misclassify the product tree or weaken tests.

payload.reason: BI-F3422349 (Vitest bound) presents a valid, complete acceptance manifest: three OBJ markers (OBJ-BOUND, OBJ-FINALIZE, OBJ-EVIDENCE) are each covered by the four AC rows (AC-VITEST-ONLY→OBJ-BOUND; AC-TREE-CLOSE and AC-NON-PASS→OBJ-FINALIZE; AC-RETRY-RECEIPT→OBJ-EVIDENCE), with no dangling ACs and no uncovered OBJs. The bounded Vitest contract is fail-closed: only the attempt runner is bounded (positive DPF_LOCAL_CI_VITEST_MAX_DURATION_MS or 1,800,000ms) with the observer unbounded; only an early 0 is passed; a real test-failure is test-failure with no retry (no masking); any non-clean result (nonzero/signal/spawn/deadline/late-0/stop/no-close) is runner-termination+retry; the finalizer escalates SIGTERM→SIGKILL on a 10s grace with a close-timeout termination guard; the second attempt is exit86+exhausted; and the receipt is released in finally. Scope is bounded to Vitest only with an explicit no-other-stage/test/schema/lease/tree guard, so there is no scope widening. This matches the authoritative canonical profile fix (workType=bug); no critical or important findings.

items.title: Preserve initiative organization authority through external reviewer approval replay
items.body:
## Problem

A commit-bound external initiative reviewer can create and receive human approval for `record_initiative_evidence`, but the approved replay writes `AuthorizationDecisionLog.organizationId = null` even when the governed backlog item belongs to an organization. The receipt repository correctly rejects the write with `Reviewer authority does not match the initiative organization`, leaving readiness permanently blocked.

## Evidence

Task `TR-MCP-Y210Nmg3bjg3MDBnYTAxbXhheDU2MXV2aQ-81B91B05D72C` targeted `BI-MCP-EFF-0285909C` at immutable commit `a08cf14638a5ee4445ddaa43beebff30f88500d2`. Its envelope was approved, then exact idempotent replay reached the writer and failed. The backlog item organization is `ORG-1787529949989` (`rescue`); both the require-approval and allow authority decisions had a null organization.

## Scope

Propagate the governed initiative organization into the external reviewer TaskRun authority context and both the approval-envelope and approved-replay decisions. Preserve immutable binding, idempotency, independent-reviewer identity, and tenant isolation. Do not weaken receipt-repository organization checks or introduce an override.

## Acceptance criteria

- The initial bound reviewer tool call records a require-approval decision with the initiative organization.
- Exact replay after employee approval records an allow decision with the same organization and executes the writer once.
- A mismatched organization remains denied.
- Idempotent replay cannot change organization, artifact, reviewer, gate, or input identity.
- Tests cover organization-bound, platform-null, mismatch, and approval-resume paths.

Blocks: BI-MCP-EFF-0285909C and all organization-bound initiatives using external readiness reviewers.

Discovered while delivering the resilient gate-flow control program.

items.title: Release publisher omits the promoter contract digest
items.body:
## Problem

The verified release pipeline publishes `dpf-promoter` without passing `DPF_PROMOTER_CONTRACT_DIGEST`. `Dockerfile.promoter` therefore leaves `org.opendpf.promoter.contract-digest=unknown`, and the governed consumer self-upgrade correctly rejects the candidate before quiescence with:

`promoter-readiness-failed: promoter_contract_digest_mismatch`

## Reproduction and evidence

1. Release `v2026.08.24-review-routing.1` at `9329979b6b62308a8fbdf4081d4fc9f19762bffb` passed publication workflow 32693132144.
2. The install initially failed because its pre-transition host state lacked `runtime-transition.secret`. The repository-pinned idempotent initializer created that file with a valid 64-hex value and owner-only Windows ACL; no existing secret was overwritten.
3. Retried run `SUR-8A34EF7B` cleared the zero-second signing-context failure, entered candidate preflight, and failed after 8 seconds with `promoter_contract_digest_mismatch`.
4. Source inspection shows `.github/workflows/publish-image.yml` passes only `DPF_VERSION` and `DPF_PLATFORM_VERSION`. It does not compute or pass `DPF_PROMOTER_CONTRACT_DIGEST`, although `Dockerfile.promoter` and `resolveCandidatePromoterArtifact` require the label to equal the SHA-256 of the embedded `/app/promoter-contract.json`.

## Scope

In scope: make the canonical release publisher compute the exact promoter-contract digest once, pass it only to the promoter build, and deterministically verify the published promoter label against the embedded manifest before E2E promotion.

Out of scope: weakening runtime artifact verification, editing the installed Compose/runtime as source, emergency drain override, or changing registry-channel discovery being developed separately under BI-C3B0B2EA.

## Acceptance criteria

- A first-failing workflow/contract test proves the promoter matrix build receives `DPF_PROMOTER_CONTRACT_DIGEST=sha256:<64 hex>`.
- Non-promoter images retain their existing build arguments and behavior.
- Publication verifies the promoter OCI contract label against the embedded manifest before the release can reach E2E or `latest`.
- Targeted tests and workflow lint pass deterministically.
- A corrected release is built through the canonical workflow.
- Governed run from `d104cd37c99ef85c8f8df5acfcd267bf1ff446a7` to the corrected release completes without emergency override.
- Canonical preflight reports CAN-TEST for `9329979b6b62308a8fbdf4081d4fc9f19762bffb` or its merge-containing corrected release commit.

## Links

- Existing consumer upgrade contract: BI-89887875
- Separate registry-channel work: BI-C3B0B2EA / WC-5F8A1DA1
- Failed run: SUR-8A34EF7B
- Release workflow: https://github.com/OpenDigitalProductFactory/opendigitalproductfactory/actions/runs/32693132144

items.title: Replace nonproduction lease polling with durable wait and resume
items.body:
## Problem

Nonproduction admission currently depends on task-local claim/list/renew polling. The efficiency scanner measured 498 claim calls with 473 estimated as waste; related list and renew items add 799 calls and 749 estimated waste. Waiting Node runners and agent turns consume memory, tokens, and coordination time.

## Scope

Represent queued admission as durable NonProductionEnvironmentLease plus Workroom/TaskRun wait state. Emit capacity transitions through existing QueueTelemetryEvent/Inngest infrastructure and deliver wakeups through DPF SSE, MCP Task subscriptions, a Codex host adapter, or a bounded reconciliation fallback. The awakened client performs one fresh host-pressure-aware claim; the event never grants admission.

## Acceptance criteria

- A queued task checkpoints and terminates its polling runner/active turn.
- Release/expiry emits an idempotent capacity-available event targeted to the FIFO head.
- Wake adapters carry lease, claim, owner-session, immutable candidate, and event identity.
- The client re-reads state and performs one fresh claim.
- Lost events are repaired by low-frequency bounded reconciliation.
- Queued liveness is server-owned; it does not depend on rapid client TTL refresh.
- Wait-related MCP call volume falls at least 95% without weakening pressure admission.

Parent: BI-7C1F43E3.
Independent delivery slice after the event contract is specified.
